strengths: Principled theoretical formulation: the fusion objective is cleanly decomposed into grouping error and approximation error (Theorem 1), yielding an interpretable two-stage algorithm; Theorem 2 provides exact optimality for the Hungarian variant and a (9+ε)-approximation guarantee for the K-means variant under affine layers, which is a meaningful theoretical contribution rarely seen in this literature.

The framework generalizes to arbitrary differentiable architectures (MLPs, CNNs, ViTs) via the flexible 'level' abstraction, avoiding the architecture-specific adaptations required by OTFusion for transformers.

Novel and well-motivated incorporation of neuron importance/attribution scores (Conductance, DeepLIFT) into the fusion objective, and the paper shows this idea can be retrofitted into existing baselines (Git Re-Basin) with benefit, which strengthens the significance of the contribution beyond just the new method.

Broad and carefully designed experimental suite spanning non-IID, sharded, and full-dataset regimes, multiple split counts, two architectures (VGG11, ViT) and two datasets (CIFAR-10/100), with results averaged over multiple seeds and reported with standard deviations.

Good-faith reproducibility effort: detailed appendices cover data partitioning schemes, training hyperparameters, fusion hyperparameters (two named settings), runtime comparisons, and licenses for reused code/assets.
Honest and specific discussion of limitations (hyperparameter sensitivity of the gradient variant, data-dependence of gradient fusion) rather than vague boilerplate limitations.
weaknesses: The gradient-based variant requires two very different, hand-picked hyperparameter 'settings' applied inconsistently across experiments (Setting 1 for full-dataset/sharded, Setting 2 for most non-IID cases) without a principled selection rule, which undermines claims of practical robustness/generality and complicates reproducibility for new settings.

Several baseline comparisons are incomplete: OTFusion/Git Re-Basin are only evaluated in the pairwise (2-way) case and marked N/A for 4-way/8-way splits since they are inherently pairwise, but this leaves gaps in table completeness; the intended comparison to Transformer OTFusion (Imfeld et al. 2023) could not be run due to implementation difficulties, so ViT-scale comparisons to a natural strong baseline are largely qualitative/anecdotal ("<12% accuracy").

Runtime analysis (Table 6) shows the K-means Linear variant is roughly 100x slower than OTFusion/Git Re-Basin, and this substantial computational overhead is not adequately weighed against the accuracy gains in the main text discussion of practical trade-offs.

Federated learning baselines (FedAvg, FedMA) that are discussed at length in Related Work are never empirically benchmarked, despite non-IID/federated fusion being a central motivating use case of the paper.

Ensemble performance remains a substantial upper bound not closely approached by any zero-shot fusion method in the more extreme non-IID/sharded/many-way splits, tempering the practical significance of the gains claimed.

The K-means approximation guarantee, while theoretically interesting, only applies to purely affine/linear levels and gives a fairly loose (9+ε) bound; its practical relevance for the non-linear/gradient-based variant actually used in most experiments is unclear.

Level partitioning (e.g., which layers to group for ViTs vs. VGGs) is done manually/heuristically per architecture, and the paper acknowledges this is not yet automated, limiting the 'plug-and-play' generality implied by the framing of the method as applicable to 'arbitrary layer types.'

strengths: Provides a principled theoretical framework: fusion is cast as a representation-matching problem with a clean grouping-error/approximation-error decomposition (Theorem 1) and formal approximation guarantees for the proposed algorithms (Theorem 2, including a (9+ε)-approximation bound for K-means Fusion), which is more rigorous than most prior fusion heuristics.

Broad empirical validation spanning multiple architectures (VGG11, ResNets 18/34/50, ViT) and datasets (CIFAR-10/100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-1k, BloodMNIST) and multiple realistic fusion regimes (full-dataset, non-IID, extreme sharded/class-disjoint, real-world medical imaging split).

Consistent and often large empirical gains over strong baselines (OTFusion, Git Re-Basin, ZipIt!, KD, LP) precisely in the zero-shot/non-IID setting that the paper identifies as underexplored, including cases where baselines collapse to near-random accuracy while the proposed methods retain substantial accuracy.

Useful ablations and analyses: effect of neuron importance scoring on clustering (with quantitative Rand-index comparisons), sensitivity to fusion dataset size and mitigation via augmentation, robustness to different model widths, runtime breakdowns showing fusion overhead is small relative to fine-tuning, and a loss-landscape visualization supporting the claim of flatter fused minima.
Practical extension to model compression via retrofitting (teacher-to-smaller-student), showing meaningful gains over KD with limited data, broadening the applicability of the framework.

Reasonably transparent about limitations (hyperparameter sensitivity, data efficiency, runtime overhead) and provides an open-source reimplementation aimed at improving reproducibility across the field.
weaknesses: The gradient-based variants (HF/KF-Gradient), which perform best in many experiments, require per-level SGD over a labeled/representative fusion dataset for up to 100 epochs, which is a substantially heavier procedure than the label of "zero-shot" fusion suggests when compared to single-pass OT/permutation methods; this added cost and complexity is somewhat under-emphasized relative to the accuracy gains reported.

Theorem 2's guarantees hold only per-level with all preceding levels fixed (greedy composition); there is no analysis of how approximation/grouping errors compound across levels for deep networks, leaving the end-to-end quality of the fused model without formal guarantees.

Results are inconsistent regarding which variant (HF vs KF, Uniform vs Conductance vs DeepLIFT) is best across settings (e.g., Table 2, Table 18), and the paper does not offer principled guidance for a practitioner to select among these many variants a priori.

The claim of being architecture-agnostic ("any modularizable architecture") is only empirically validated on three closely related vision architectures (VGG, ResNet, ViT); no experiments on other modalities (e.g., LLMs, RNNs, graph networks) are provided, despite this being highlighted as a key contribution.

Runtime costs for the linear variants (especially KF-Linear) are substantially higher than lightweight baselines (e.g., 78s vs 0.7s for OTFusion on VGG), and while the paper argues this is amortized against fine-tuning cost in full-dataset settings, this may not hold for very large-scale models where fusion itself could become a bottleneck.

The claim in the conclusion of being "the first to successfully incorporate neuron importance scores" is in some tension with the paper's own discussion (Section C) that OTFusion already incorporates importance as a transport probability measure; the novelty framing could be more precise.

Some result tables (e.g., Table 2, Table 17) are dense and awkwardly formatted with multiple individual-model accuracies crammed together, reducing readability and making it harder to verify comparisons at a glance.

Direct empirical comparison with FL-specific baselines mentioned in the introduction (FedAvg, FedMA) is discussed conceptually but not included in the main quantitative benchmarks, despite the paper's framing around FL-relevant non-IID settings.
